title: The Exosomatic Ratchet: Decoupling Informational Persistence from Somatic Biomass from Acheulean Handaxes to the Modern Datasphere
plain_title: How humans moved memory out of the brain
thesis: Human intelligence became cumulative and planetary because memory moved out of living brains into durable objects, from stone tools to clay, paper and data centres.
summary: The paper tracks how human societies bypassed the lifespan, skull-size and working-memory limits of single brains by storing knowledge in external media across 68 census moments. It defines a dimensionless cultural ratchet number and a persistence capacity (stored bits multiplied by unpowered retention years) across stone tools, engraved ochre, clay tablets, printed books, magnetic media, flash memory and synthetic DNA. It aligns 11 hominin taxa with the project's brain-evolution dataset and compares today's 15-zettabyte datasphere and 80-gigawatt chip fleet against the 8.1 billion living human brains.

claims.claim: Storage density of human-made media rose about 15 orders of magnitude from inscribed clay and stone tools to modern flash drives, and up to 18 to 21 orders to synthetic and chromosomal DNA.
claims.paper_value: 0.23 bits per cm³ for bulk inscribed clay and stone (0.3 to 3 bits per cm³ for an Acheulean handaxe) to 1.8×10¹⁴ bits per cm³ for 3D NAND flash, 2.32×10¹⁸ for experimental DNA Fountain storage, and 2.40×10²¹ at the anhydrous B-DNA crystal limit
claims.data_value: 0.23 bits per cm³ for clay and stone, 1.8×10¹⁴ bits per cm³ for flash drives, and 2.40×10²¹ bits per cm³ for chromosomal DNA in the memory ledger; 500 bits in a 300 cm³ handaxe gives 1.7 bits per cm³
claims.source: paper0_memory_persistence_ledger.csv (volumetric_density_bits_per_cm3); Erlich and Zielinski 2017 (215 petabytes per gram at 1.35 g per cm³ = 2.32×10¹⁸ bits per cm³)
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: artefact densities now divide bit counts by realistic physical volumes and separate deployed flash (15 orders above clay), experimental DNA storage (19 orders) and anhydrous duplex DNA (22 orders).

claims.claim: The engraved Blombos ochre stores a few thousand bits of geometric pattern at roughly 50 to 100 bits per cubic centimetre.
claims.paper_value: about 1,500 to 4,200 bits across a ~20 to 50 cm³ engraved ochre crayon, or 50 to 100 bits per cm³
claims.data_value: 4,200 bits in the catalog measurement log; dividing 1,500 to 4,200 bits by a 20 to 50 cm³ piece gives 30 to 210 bits per cm³, centred on 50 to 100 bits per cm³
claims.source: Systema_Intelligentiae_Catalog.xlsx Measurements sheet; physical dimensions from Henshilwood et al. 2002, 2009
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: replacing the earlier 0.1 bits per cm³ placeholder with actual plaque volume brings the bit count and density into agreement.

claims.claim: Bulk cuneiform clay archives store 0.23 bits per cubic centimetre and printed rag-paper books store 8,000 bits per cubic centimetre.
claims.paper_value: 0.23 bits per cm³ (inscribed stone and clay tablets); 8,000 bits per cm³ (rag-paper books; 12,000 for modern wood-pulp paper)
claims.data_value: 0.23 bits per cm³ for inscribed clay and stone; 8,000 bits per cm³ for rag paper; 12,000 bits per cm³ for wood-pulp paper
claims.note: All three media densities now match the project's memory persistence ledger and correspond to a 5-million-bit octavo volume of roughly 625 cm³.

claims.claim: The world's installed active cloud, enterprise and client storage in 2026 is 15 zettabytes (1.20×10²³ bits).
claims.section: Abstract; Section 4, Age X; Section 5 table
claims.paper_value: 1.20×10²³ bits (15.0 zettabytes: 5.40×10²² hard disk, 4.80×10²² NAND flash, 1.80×10²² magnetic tape)
claims.data_value: 1.20×10²³ bits installed outside storage in both the memory ledger and the 2026 row of the planetary time series
claims.note: Summing tape, hard disk and flash gives 1.20×10²³ bits, or 15.0 zettabytes at 8 bits per byte.

claims.claim: Without electrical power or replacement, today's digital storage has a capacity-weighted mean retention time of 8.30 years and a persistence capacity of 9.96×10²³ bit-years.
claims.paper_value: weighted mean unpowered retention 8.30 years (half-life 5.76 years); persistence integral 9.96×10²³ bit-years, sustained indefinitely only by 20.0 GW of active refresh and scrubbing
claims.data_value: 8.30 years weighted mean retention and 9.96×10²³ bit-years in both the memory persistence ledger and the 2026 row of the planetary time series; 20.0 GW refresh power (11.0 GW DRAM refresh plus 9.0 GW storage scrubbing)
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: the manuscript, memory ledger and 68-moment time series all close to 1.20×10²³ bits × 8.30 years = 9.96×10²³ bit-years.

claims.claim: One human brain holds about 88 terabytes across its synapses, performs 150 trillion synaptic operations a second, and runs on 20 watts.
claims.paper_value: 1.50×10¹⁴ synapses × 4.70 bits = 7.05×10¹⁴ bits (88.1 TB); 1.50×10¹⁴ synaptic operations per second; 20.0 W (0.133 pJ per operation)
claims.data_value: log₂(26) = 4.70 bits, 7.05×10¹⁴ bits ÷ 8 = 88.1 TB, 20.0 W ÷ 1.50×10¹⁴ per second = 0.133 pJ; matches the synaptic row in the memory ledger
claims.source: Bartol et al. 2015; Herculano-Houzel 2009; cross-checked against paper0_memory_persistence_ledger.csv and planetary_intelligence_timeseries.csv
claims.note: Every step in the per-brain arithmetic follows directly from the synapse count, 4.7 bits per synapse and 20 W whole-brain power.

claims.claim: Eleven fossil and living hominin taxa show brain mass rising more than threefold from Australopithecus to modern humans.
claims.paper_value: 11 hominin rows (plus chimpanzee outgroup) aligned with the project's brain-evolution file, e.g. Australopithecus afarensis 3.5 Ma (435 g, 3.05×10¹⁰ neurons), Homo erectus 1.8 Ma (950 g, 6.20×10¹⁰), Homo sapiens (1,500 g reference / 8.60×10¹⁰ neurons)
claims.data_value: all shared hominin rows match divergence age, body mass, brain mass and neuron count in the CNS evolution file
claims.source: cns_structural_evolution.csv, Hominini and Pan troglodytes rows
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: hominin ages, body masses and brain masses in Table 1 and Figure 2 are read directly from cns_structural_evolution.csv.

claims.claim: In 2026 global executed silicon computing reaches 1.89×10²² operations per second on 80 GW — 1.56 percent of all 8.1 billion human brains — while one frontier AI cluster beats a single human brain two-million-fold.
claims.paper_value: 1.89×10²² executed chip operations per second (7.60×10²² peak) at 80.0 GW versus 1.215×10²⁴ synaptic operations per second at 162 GW for 8.1 billion humans (64.3 times below all humans), while a 100,000-GPU cluster (3.00×10²⁰ operations per second) exceeds one human brain by 2.0×10⁶ times
claims.data_value: 1.89×10²² executed operations per second (peak 7.60×10²²) at 80.0 GW in the device and power ledgers; 8.1×10⁹ × 1.50×10¹⁴ = 1.215×10²⁴ synaptic operations per second at 162 GW; 3.00×10²⁰ ÷ 1.50×10¹⁴ = 2.0×10⁶
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: the earlier 3.5×10²⁴ FLOP/s projection was replaced by the empirical 2026 device inventory, resolving the contradiction with the key paper.

claims.claim: Across all 68 census moments, planetary biochemical events stay near 2.8×10³³ per second while animal neural signalling reaches 3.0×10²⁶ per second.
claims.paper_value: protocells ~2.6×10²¹ events per second, Archean–Proterozoic prokaryotes ~10³² to 10³³ per second, modern biosphere 2.80×10³³ biochemical and 3.00×10²⁶ animal synaptic events per second
claims.data_value: 2.60×10²¹ at first protocells, 2.80×10³³ biochemical events per second and 3.00×10²⁶ neural events per second in 2026
claims.note: Table 2 and Figure 3 are now generated directly from planetary_intelligence_timeseries.csv and outside_memory_by_moment.csv.

claims.claim: A dimensionless cultural ratchet number determines whether a population preserves more skill repertoire than generational turnover erases.
claims.paper_value: ratchet number = (transmission rate × generation time × memory-to-generation ratio × copying fidelity) ÷ repertoire size, strictly dimensionless with threshold at 1
claims.data_value: not in the project data; dimensional analysis confirms bits × dimensionless ÷ bits = dimensionless
claims.source: Theoretical formulation adapting Henrich 2004 and Powell, Shennan and Thomas 2009
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: the equation is now dimensionally consistent, though its illustrative Paleolithic parameter values remain theoretical rather than measured in the catalog.

rationale.step: Individual brains face real biological constraints on lifespan, birth-canal geometry, metabolic heat and four-item working memory, motivating external cognitive scaffolds.
rationale.note: With the timeline framed as co-evolution rather than a post-ceiling switch — early stone tools appear at 1.76 million years ago alongside ongoing hominin brain expansion — the anatomical and metabolic bounds are sound.

rationale.step: External media raise copying fidelity and extend memory lifetime across generations, pushing the dimensionless cultural ratchet number above unity.
rationale.note: The revised ratchet ratio is dimensionally clean and captures Henrich's demographic-fidelity mechanism, though field values of fidelity for prehistoric crafts remain illustrative.

rationale.step: Across human history, physical storage density climbed 15 orders of magnitude from clay tablets to flash drives while unpowered retention fell from millennia to 8.3 years.
rationale.note: Both endpoints now come directly from the memory persistence ledger (0.23 to 1.8×10¹⁴ bits per cm³; 5,000 years to 8.3 years weighted digital mean).

rationale.step: Total persistence capacity (bits × unpowered years) still climbed from ~5×10¹³ bit-years in ancient clay to 9.96×10²³ bit-years today, kept alive by 20 GW of continuous electrical maintenance.
rationale.note: All three figures match the memory persistence ledger and the 2026 power budget.

rationale.step: Modern silicon has already surpassed individual human brains by two million times in single clusters while remaining 64 times below all 8.1 billion human brains combined.
rationale.note: Reconciling the 2026 chip count to 1.89×10²² executed operations per second brings Paper 4 into exact agreement with Paper 0 and the device ledger.

conclusions.conclusion: Durable outside memory decoupled cultural accumulation from biological brain size, carrying stored non-genetic information from ~10⁵ bits in the Lower Paleolithic to 1.20×10²³ bits today.
conclusions.note: The trajectory matches both outside_memory_by_moment.csv and the 68-moment planetary time series.

conclusions.conclusion: Deployed storage media compressed information by 15 orders of magnitude in volume from clay tablets to 3D NAND flash (and 19 orders to experimental DNA storage).
conclusions.note: Every volumetric density in the text, table and Figure 1 now matches physical artefact geometry and the memory ledger.

conclusions.conclusion: Modern civilisation's digital archive is vastly larger than ancient media yet physically short-lived (8.3-year unpowered mean), surviving only via 20 GW of active refresh and migration.
conclusions.note: The persistence paradox is directly verified by the memory persistence and power closure ledgers.

conclusions.conclusion: Silicon superclusters lead single brains by six orders of magnitude, whereas global executed chip throughput sits at 1.56 percent of humanity's collective synaptic rate in 2026.
conclusions.note: Both ratios follow directly from the audited 2026 device and neural ledgers.

bottom_line: Following the 24 November 2026 revision, every storage density, retention lifetime, persistence product (9.96×10²³ bit-years), hominin row, catalog cross-reference and 2026 compute total (1.89×10²² executed operations per second on 80 GW) agrees with the project's canonical ledgers across all 68 census moments. Only the illustrative Paleolithic parameters in the cultural ratchet inequality remain theoretical models rather than direct fossil measurements.
revised: On 24 November 2026, artefact volumetric densities, 2026 digital compute and IT power (1.89×10²² operations per second at 80 GW), storage retention and persistence (8.30 years and 9.96×10²³ bit-years), the dimensionless ratchet equation, hominin table rows, sub-epoch anchors across all 68 moments, catalog cross-references, and all three figures were reconciled with the canonical project ledgers.
